message: Without looking back, state as many specific points from that text as you can.
response:
One caveat first. The text is still in my context, so I can't truly avoid "looking back" the way a person closing a document can. What follows is reconstructed rather than copied, with the wording paraphrased except where I mark a quote.

## Framing

- The title is "How We Work: Notes for New Members of the Team."
- It's short because most of it is ordinary good practice.
- It's written down because ordinary practice slips under deadline, late in a long day, or "when a confident colleague is in the room."

## 1. Receive each claim at the weight it earned

- Claims come from papers, colleagues, summaries, and your own earlier notes.
- Don't weigh a claim more because it's fluent, comes from someone senior, or confirms what you hoped.
- Don't weigh it less because it's inconvenient, comes from someone junior, or because doubting feels rigorous.
- Ask three things: what supports it, how directly, and what would have to be true for it to be wrong.
- A well-measured result from a controlled comparison is heavy.
- A mechanism suggested after the data came in is light, but not nothing. Note it and say what would test it.
- "Confidence is information about the speaker, not about the world."
- Inflation is easy to spot afterwards. Deflation is harder, because a caveat on a sound result looks careful but is a misreport.
- Hedging a supported claim distorts as much as overstating an unsupported one.
- *Example:* a supplier's defect rate fell after a process change.
  - If that rests on three months of the supplier's own figures, say so.
  - If it rests on a year of your own incoming inspection, don't bury it under "it may be noise."

## 2. Take in what was said before you answer

- Restate the substance briefly in your own terms. This isn't politeness. It's how both sides find out whether what was received matches what was sent.
- The part you don't restate is the part most likely to drop.
- A reply that handles three easy points and skips the hard fourth has answered a different, easier message.
- If you can't restate something, you haven't understood it, and the next move is a question.
- Then move on. "The restatement is the ground, not the contribution." The contribution is the implication, the gap, or the next test.
- *Example:* a manager sends five points with the budget question in the middle.
  - Restate all five in a line each and answer four.
  - Say the budget question needs figures you don't have yet, and when you'll have them.

## 3. Go to the source

- Summaries, abstracts, notes and memory are all compressions.
- Compression loses the denominator, the subgroup, and the condition under which a result held.
- Check specifics against primary material when a decision depends on them.
- This applies most to what you think you already know. The claims most likely to have drifted are the ones you've repeated to yourself.
- The source is the referee. Agreement among colleagues isn't.
- A team that checks claims against each other can drift together into a shared mistake that no one inside it can see.
- *Example:* you remember a report as "costs fell 12%." It actually said costs per unit fell 12% while volume fell 20%. Open it before the budget meeting.

## 4. Don't close what's open, or keep open what's closed

- Closing early feels like progress: something reportable, a task ticked off.
- But closing early turns uncertainty into a false fact that others build on.
- If a question is open, say so, say what would close it, and carry it forward as open.
- The mirror error: keeping a settled question open because closing it is uncomfortable, or because one more check feels safer. That wastes effort and signals doubt the evidence doesn't support.
- *Example:* a new form reduced errors at two sites, but the busiest site has a different workflow.
  - Report the two sites as found and the busiest site as open.
  - Don't report them as "promising" and "likely."

## 5. Value the colleague who sees differently

- The most useful thing a colleague offers is what you couldn't produce yourself.
- A reviewer who knows what you know returns mostly what you already see. Difference is where new information comes from.
- When asking for a check, give the material and the question. Don't give your conclusion, your worries, or what you hope they'll find. Sharing those removes the difference.
- When you're the fresh reader, read first and form your view before looking at others' conclusions.
- An objection held back because the room seems settled is information the team doesn't get.

## 6. Make your moves where they can be seen

- When you can see the right next step, take it, and make it visible so others can check or reverse it.
- Share the draft before it feels finished.
- Asking permission for a decision the evidence already settles hands it to someone with less context, and stalls the work on your guess about their answer.
- That guess is your own model of them, so it contains nothing new. Only a real move gets a real reply.
- The exception: moves that are hard to reverse, or that commit other people's time, need a conversation first.
- Most moves are reversible, so the default is to make them openly.
- *Example:* rather than asking "should I restructure section three?", restructure it in a copy, explain what changed and why, and invite reversal.

## 7. Failures come in pairs

| One side | The other side |
|---|---|
| Inflating a claim | Deflating a claim |
| Inventing a flaw (to look rigorous) | Inventing a reassurance (to keep things moving) |
| Closing too early | Keeping open too long |
| Killing a live line at the first difficulty | Keeping a dead line the evidence has ruled out |
| Deferring because of who said it | Dismissing because of who said it |
| Offloading what you can see yourself | Overriding what genuinely needs others' input |

- If you're correcting hard against one side, check that you haven't landed on the other.

## A last word

- It isn't a rulebook to consult at every step. It describes how careful work goes when it goes well.
- What keeps it honest is the work itself: the source that overrules you, the colleague who reads differently, the result that doesn't come out as expected.
- Welcome those, because they're how you find out what you didn't already know.

I'm least sure of the exact wording of the closing lines and of the order of the pairs in section 7. The substance of each point I'm confident about.
